The conference brought together chiefs of defense and senior military leaders from 29 countries under the theme “Strengthening Collective Security: Navigating Challenges in a Dynamic Indo-Pacific Landscape.” US PACOM is committed to enhancing stability in the region by promoting security cooperation, encouraging peaceful development, responding to contingencies, and deterring aggression. Adm. Samuel J. Paparo, commander of U.S. Pacific Command, met with senior military leaders and representatives from across the Indo-Pacific and beyond on the sidelines of the 28th Indo-Pacific Chiefs of Defense Conference in Victoria, Canada, Aug. 31-Sept. 2.

Paparo emphasized the importance of strong bilateral and multilateral relationships in advancing regional security and deterrence.

During the conference, Paparo participated in meetings of the Defense Cooperation Council and the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue and joined military leaders from ASEAN nations. Paparo also spoke with counterparts from the United Kingdom and Australia for an AUKUS conversation and met with Adm. Giuseppe Cavo Dragone, chair of the NATO Military Committee.

Discussing shared security interests, Paparo held bilateral meetings with a number of senior leaders representing countries including Bangladesh, Brunei, Cambodia, Canada, France, India, Indonesia, Japan, Malaysia, Mexico, Mongolia, New Zealand, the Republic of Korea, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam. The meetings focused on strengthening operational cooperation, information-sharing, maritime security and readiness across the Indo-Pacific.

Paparo met with Maj. Gen. Pawan Raj Ghimire, general officer commanding of the Nepali Army’s Eastern Division, to express his condolences following the recent disaster in Nepal.

Paparo also met with Gen. Yang Zhibin, commander of the People’s Liberation Army’s Eastern Theater Command, marking their first in-person meeting. The two leaders discussed the importance of maintaining open lines of communication between senior U.S. and Chinese military leaders to reduce the risk of miscalculation and promote safe and professional conduct between forces.

On Sep. 3, at the direction of U.S. Southern Command Commander Gen. Francis L. Donovan, and in coordination and collaboration with the Government of Ecuador, Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere (JTF-WHEM) successfully interdicted a vessel operating as a floating refueling station in support of illicit at-sea drug trafficking operations in international waters of the Eastern Pacific. Intelligence confirmed the vessel was operating in support of the Los Choneros violent narco-terrorist organization. Littoral Combat Force 24 launched from USS San Antonio (LPD 17), interdicted, boarded, searched, and cleared the vessel without incident. Individuals removed from the vessel will be safely transferred to Ecuadorian authorities. Once cleared, U.S. forces sank the vessel. This interdiction cuts off a critical node in the traffickers' logistics chain and advances the goals of the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition (A3C) and JTF-WHEM to dismantle narco-terrorist networks. The Department of War and the A3C remain unwavering in their mission to defeat narco-terrorists in the Western Hemisphere and defend our homeland.

items.title: Camp Parks, Alameda County team up to battle 1,000-acre wildfire
items.author: Jim O'Donnell
items.summary: When a fast-moving wildland fire threatened structures and powerlines near Sunol, California, July 21, 2026, the Camp Parks Fire Department did not hesitate to answer the call. Demonstrating the vital strength of regional emergency partnerships, the Camp Parks Fire Department deployed crucial resources to assist regional agencies in containing the "Little Fire," which scorched over 1,007 acres of grass and brush in Alameda County.
items.body:
Photo By Jim O'Donnell | Camp Parks firefighters in Water Tender 44, approach a boundary of the Little Fire,... ... read more read more

Photo By Jim O'Donnell | Camp Parks firefighters in Water Tender 44, approach a boundary of the Little Fire, July 21, 2026, in support of Alameda County Fire Department and California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection. The PRFTA Fire Department response is a facet of the Intergovernmental Service Agreement between PRFTA and Alameda County that allows Camp Parks and Alameda County emergency services to seamlessly provide mutual aid to one another during large-scale emergencies. (Photo courtesy of Camp Parks Fire Department) see less | View Image Page

DUBLIN, Calif. — When a fast-moving wildland fire threatened structures and powerlines near Sunol, California, July 21, 2026, the Camp Parks Fire Department did not hesitate to answer the call. Demonstrating the vital strength of regional emergency partnerships, the Camp Parks Fire Department deployed crucial resources to assist regional agencies in containing the "Little Fire," which scorched over 1,007 acres of grass and brush in Alameda County. The fire, which erupted at 3:39 p.m. near Vallecitos Road and Little Valley Road, quickly expanded into a remote area characterized by difficult access and steep terrain, according to the Alameda County Fire Department website. Fueled by dry vegetation and challenging summer weather, the blaze grew to 700 acres within hours, prompting immediate evacuation orders and warnings from local authorities. Responding under an established Intragovernmental Support Agreement (IGSA) with Alameda County, Camp Parks Fire Department dispatched Water Tender 44 (WT-44) and a dedicated crew of firefighters to the scene that afternoon. The cooperative agreement allows Camp Parks and Alameda County emergency services to seamlessly provide mutual aid to one another during large-scale emergencies. "Our partnership with Alameda County is a lifeline, not just for the garrison, but for the entire community," said Lt. Col. Tony Ibrahim, Camp Parks garrison commander. "Knowing we have a highly trained, rapid-response firefighting team on Camp Parks that can integrate instantly with our civilian counterparts gives us immense pride and peace of mind. Our firefighters performed exceptionally well alongside Alameda County Fire Department and the California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection (CAL FIRE) to keep our neighbors safe." Fighting on difficult terrain The Little Fire presented significant challenges to the hundreds of first responders on the ground and in the air. High temperatures, limited access roads, and volatile fuel conditions forced a robust, multi-agency response. CAL FIRE Santa Clara Unit and Alameda County Fire Department entered Unified Command to battle the flames, deploying ground engines, hand crews, bulldozers, air tankers, and helicopters. For the leadership overseeing the initial dispatch and operational response, joint training made all the difference. "Coordination on the ground was seamless because we train for these exact scenarios with our Alameda County partners," said Navin Basilio, Camp Parks firefighting supervisor. Among those on the front lines battling the blaze were the engine crews who directly confronted the challenging conditions and logistical constraints in the Sunol hills. "Access was limited, as well as resources; this required constant communication and the ability to remain flexible as needs arose with ACFD and Cal Fire," said Justin Chiappetta, a Camp Parks firefighter who responded to the incident. "Water Tender 44 (WT-44) holds 3,000 gallons of water and has limited off-road capabilities, so we were assigned to a location where the terrain was manageable to drive while still being able to give water to the vehicles fighting the fire." Alongside Chiappetta, other members of the Camp Parks crew worked diligently to support the fast-moving firefight. Despite the difficult conditions, which included a non-fatal CAL FIRE engine rollover that resulted in minor injuries to one firefighter, the collaborative response quickly yielded results. By the morning of July 22, forward progress of the fire was successfully halted at 1,007 acres, allowing crews to shift their focus to strengthening containment lines and patrolling for active hot spots. By July 25, the incident commander reported 100 percent containment, and all evacuation orders were lifted. A reciprocal lifeline The mutual aid provided during the Little Fire represents a reciprocal relationship that has protected both federal property and civilian communities. Nearly a year prior, the value of the IGSA#_msocom_1 was demonstrated in reverse when the "Parks Fire" erupted on Camp Parks on Aug. 22, 2025. Starting in the afternoon that day, the wildland fire that began in the training area north of Camp Parks cantonment area, threatened the military installation, prompting a rapid, coordinated response. Under the jurisdiction of the Alameda County Fire Department, civilian firefighting assets—including ground engines, air assets, and support crews—rushed to the training area. Working hand-in-hand with Camp Parks firefighters, regional crews successfully battled the blaze. Through this unified effort, the fire was fully contained by 8 p.m. on Aug. 25, 2025, preventing it from crossing boundaries into neighboring Dublin and San Ramon. "The seamless coordination between our departments is a testament to the strength of our mutual aid partnership," said Cory Rutherglen, division chief for the Alameda County Fire Department. "During the Little Fire, the crucial water support provided by Camp Parks' Water Tender 44 crew was vital to our operations on the ground. Similarly, when the Parks Fire threatened their installation in August 2025, our ACFD Hand Crew 8 and Dozer 17 were proud to stand side-by-side with them. We are safer and more effective because we operate as one team." "This is mutual aid in its truest form," Ibrahim said. "In August 2025, our civilian neighbors stood with us when fire threatened our training area. This July, we were honored to stand with them to defend Sunol. These actions prove that emergency safety knows no municipal boundaries."

items.title: AMC deputy commander retires after 32 years of distinguished service
items.author: 1st Lt. Kevin Powers
items.summary: Members across the mobility enterprise, family, and distinguished guests gathered here, Sept. 3, to honor Lt. Gen. Rebecca Sonkiss, Air Mobility Command deputy commander, as she retired following more than three decades of distinguished military service.

Photo By Tech. Sgt. Dalton Williams | U.S. Air Force Gen. Randall Reed, commander of U.S. Transportation Command, presents a certificate to Lt. Gen. Rebecca Sonkiss, Air Mobility Command deputy commander, during her retirement ceremony on Scott Air Force Base, Illinois, September 3, 2026. Members across the mobility enterprise, family, and distinguished guests gathered to honor Sonkiss’s strategic contributions to joint warfighting readiness and her advocacy for Airmen through 32 years of distinguished military service. (U.S. Air Force photo by Tech. Sgt. Dalton Williams) see less | View Image Page

Members across the mobility enterprise, family, and distinguished guests gathered here, Sept. 3, to honor Lt. Gen. Rebecca Sonkiss, Air Mobility Command deputy commander, as she retired following more than three decades of distinguished military service. As a command pilot, Sonkiss flew 4,598 flight hours, including 1,377 combat hours, in nine different Air Force manned and remotely piloted aircraft.

The ceremony celebrated a career defined by rapid global mobility leadership, her strategic contributions to joint warfighting readiness and her unwavering advocacy for Airmen.

Gen. Randall Reed, commander of U.S. Transportation Command, the presiding officer of the ceremony, remarked on Sonkiss’s career and lasting impact on those around her.

“You've accomplished everything that you can possibly accomplish,” said Reed. “You have taught the rest of us to take it from here.”

Sonkiss’s retirement marks the end of a pivotal chapter for AMC. In October 2024, she became the deputy commander for AMC and guided the command through the successful execution of Operation Midnight Hammer and the Department-Level Exercise series in 2025. Stepping into the role of AMC interim commander in February 2026, Sonkiss led the command through Operation Epic Fury , in addition to the delivery of critical relief in response to the earthquakes that occurred in Venezuela on June 24, 2026.

Throughout her tenure, she championed modernization of the Mobility Air Forces, focusing AMC’s efforts on https://www.mitchellaerospacepower.org/events/lt-gen-rebecca-j-sonkiss/:

“Our Airmen adapted, survived – even thrived – and enabled the Joint Force to deliver the protection the theater needed, the fuel our fighters and bombers must have and the confidence to operate at great risk,” said Sonkiss.

The retirement ceremony concluded with the traditional rendering of salutes and the presentation of major awards recognizing her decades of service. Airmen from Scott Air Force Base Honor Guard presented her with a folded American flag that belonged to her late father. In July, Sonkiss flew the flag to honor her father’s legacy during her fini flight, where she piloted a C-17 Globemaster III at Joint Base Lindsey Graham, South Carolina. Addressing the audience of Airmen, colleagues, and family, Sonkiss reflected on her final command tour and the legacy of the mobility enterprise.

“The real work of leaders is not in creating their own personal legacy. It's about investing in others,” said Sonkiss. “The legacy is creating those connections and service that make us all more capable than we believe possible. It's not my legacy; it's ours.”

Meade, Maryland, Aug. 28, 2026. Sutton visited MCIC to discuss the command’s implementation of U.S. Cyber Command’s CYBERCOM 2.0, a revised cyber force generation model that places a greater emphasis on specialized personnel and training and meet with Marines responsible for supporting the Department’s cyber mission. FORT GEORGE G. MEADE, Md. — The Honorable Katherine Sutton, Assistant Secretary of War for Cyber Policy and Principal Cyber Advisor to the Secretary of War, visited Marine Forces at Fort George G. Meade, Maryland, Aug. 28, 2026, to discuss the Department’s cyber priorities and U.S. Cyber Command’s CYBERCOM 2.0 implementation.

The visit gave Sutton an opportunity to meet with Marines and personnel responsible for carrying out department-level cyber priorities and identify areas requiring further coordination. She highlighted her vision for the Department to deliver the most capable, lethal, and agile cyber force in the world, in order to deter conflict, secure our strategic advantage, and defeat adversary aggression decisively.

She also highlighted the critical role of CYBERCOM 2.0, as it reimagines how the Department will forge and employ elite cyber warriors by placing greater emphasis on specialized personnel and training. The implementation focuses on deepening the speed and domain mastery of joint cyber capabilities while creating a structure that harmonizes collaboration throughout the force.

“The model fundamentally changes the Department’s approach to generating cyber forces, enabling increased lethality in our cyber forces and establishing a warrior ethos built on domain mastery, specialized skills, and mission agility,” Sutton said when the department announced the initiative in November of 2025.

During the visit, Sutton met with Lt. Gen. Joseph Matos III, deputy commandant for information, and Brig. Gen. Ahmed Williamson, commanding general of Marine Forces Cyberspace Command, Marine Forces Space Command, and Marine Corps Information Command. The Marine leaders gave Sutton an overview of current operations and how the command brings together capabilities across cyber, space and the information environment in support of CYBERCOM 2.0 objectives.

“The warfighting ethos and camaraderie Marines share are our greatest strengths, but we don't fight alone,” said Williamson. “We have to bring that same commitment to the joint force and work together across the services to build the most lethal cyber force possible.”

“To deter conflict and win decisively in cyberspace, we must invest deeply in our cyber forces,” said Sutton. “Our partnership with the Marine Corps is central to realizing the CYBERCOM 2.0 vision – building domain mastery, modernizing career pathways, fostering specialized skills, and delivering lethal, mission-ready cyber warriors to the joint force.”

Sutton met separately with enlisted Marines in the ranks of sergeant and below, along with officers in the ranks of captain and below. Marines provided feedback on their experiences supporting the Department’s cyber mission and implementing CYBERCOM 2.0 at the tactical level, including how training, career development and available tools affect their ability to execute the mission.

Artificial intelligence and data-driven operations were also a focus. Participants discussed how AI-enabled capabilities are being used and developed to support targeting, sensing and decision-making. The discussion also addressed what is needed to responsibly scale those capabilities.

“The future of cyber warfare depends on pairing talented warriors with agile, data-driven technologies,” said Sutton. “The speed at which Marines are operationalizing artificial intelligence provides a blueprint for the joint force, and we are committed to removing institutional barriers, so our operators have the advanced tools to outpace any adversary.”

The visit concluded with a discussion of implementation milestones and support requirements, as well as how the Marine Corps, U.S. Cyber Command, and War Department cyber policy leaders will continue to create a more lethal and masterful cyber force.

U.S. Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Ken Wilsbach and Chief Master Sergeant of the Air Force David Wolfe recently concluded a multi-day tour throughout the U.S. Central Command area of responsibility August 23-25. The visit focused on engaging with Airmen, assessing field realities, and meeting with regional air chiefs.

Throughout their travels, Wilsbach and Wolfe had an opportunity to hear directly from Airmen about conditions on the ground, understand challenges affecting mission execution, and observe how units are translating readiness into action. According to both leaders, readiness is on display every day in CENTCOM, ultimately being demonstrated through heroic actions of Airmen.

CSAF and CMSAF thanked Airmen for their warfighter mentality, commitment, and resolve required through sustained operational demands, and for remaining resilient during a period defined by uncertainty and change.

“It’s impressive to be in front of American heroes, and I don’t say that lightly,” Wilsbach told a room full of deployed Airmen. “That’s the way I view it. You’re gritty, courageous warriors fighting for our country. I’m so impressed by you, proud of you, and thankful to be on your team.”

Airmen continue operating under extraordinary demands that have required extensive use of U.S. airpower, including fighters, bombers, tankers, mobility aircraft, intelligence platforms, air defense systems and other capabilities spread across the region.

Behind every sortie and system are Airmen generating aircraft, protecting installations, moving cargo, analyzing threats, sustaining communications and solving problems under pressure.

To sustain those high-tempo operations, Wilsbach and Wolfe also focused on quality-of-life factors that directly impact the force reaffirming their commitment to deployed units.

“Each of you demonstrate unmatched courage and technical precision in the face of persistent threats," Wolfe said while meeting warfighters on the ground. "Operating in a contested environment tests our resolve, but our strength comes from you. We’re proud of you.”

The visit also prioritized coalition integration, where Wilsbach and Wolfe met with air chiefs and partner nation leadership to discuss regional stability. The engagements highlighted how partner forces are fusing readiness and lethality across a dynamic theater.

The CENTCOM visit concluded as CSAF met with leaders who are integrating airpower for major combat operations alongside regional partners.

“Our battle-tested Airmen inspire confidence in our current and future force,” said Wilsbach “The Air Component has shown up and demonstrated we’re a critical team player within the Joint Force and this region.”

PACIFIC MISSILE RANGE FACILITY, Hawaii – When a crisis strikes the remote island of Kauaʻi, the ability to respond effectively often comes down to the community’s ability to work together. For Kelly Balmores, the Emergency Management Officer (EMO) at Pacific Missile Range Facility (PMRF), Barking Sands, the connections he’s developed with his peers and neighbors prove critical in an emergency.

Born and raised on the island’s south shore in Kōloa and a graduate of Kauaʻi High School, Balmores has spent the last 15 years serving PMRF and the community, developing emergency response procedures and promoting community readiness.

After a brief stint working in local restaurants, Balmores joined the U.S. Army. Serving as a 12 Bravo combat engineer, he deployed to Iraq in August 1990 in support of Operations Desert Shield and Desert Storm. Following his military service, he transitioned to civilian law enforcement and later spent ten years with the Department of Energy (DOE).

"That's where I got into emergency response and Incident Command [JB1] Systems (ICS)," Balmores said, noting he was primarily the "boots on the ground" for DOE operations.

Balmores brought that expertise back to Kauaʻ i in 2011,[JB2] initially serving as PMRF’s Installation Training Officer. After dual-hatting for several years, he officially took lead as the installation's permanent EMO in 2018. His expertise is backed by the highly selective Navy Emergency Manager certification, a rigorous qualification requiring real-world incident experience, multiple years as an EMO and the completion of 50 s[JB3] pecific duty tasks. He is one of roughly 40 personnel enterprise-wide to hold the designation. For Balmores, successful emergency management hinges on community integration and proactive coordination.

"There's a saying out there... when an incident is occurring, that's not the time to be trading business cards," Balmores explained. Growing up on Kauaʻi gave him a unique advantage; many of PMRF’s key partners in emergency management are people that Balmores knew growing up or even went to school with. "Establishing those relationships before an emergency is important."

These lifelong relationships have proven critical during real-world crises where PMRF and the county share limited resources. During the severe 2018 rain events and landslides on the North Shore, Balmores coordinated with the county to use U.S. Navy landing craft to shuttle ambulances, bulldozers, food, and water to cut-off residents.

Similarly, during the Kaumakani fires, PMRF’s unique military resources played a pivotal role in assisting local first responders. "We brought out military aircraft with larger buckets into play, which really controlled the fire, whereas the community’s buckets were smaller," Balmores noted. "They started to get the fire under control because of a resource we were able to share to keep the community safe.”

Balmores acts as a liaison officer for the Kauaʻi Emergency Management Agency (KEMA), teaches Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) courses to local agencies, and sits as a voting member on the Local Emergency Planning Committee (LEPC). Currently, the LEPC is tackling complex island-wide challenges, such as the safe disposal of toxic electric vehicle (EV) batteries.

Whether he is planning for future hazards or responding to an immediate threat, Balmores remains motivated by a desire to help his community.

"Because we're such a small island and such a small base, whether an incident involves the county, state, or PMRF, we're partners," Balmores said.

September is National Preparedness Month and with the recent storms brewing in the Pacific it is more crucial than ever to make sure your family is prepared for an emergency. Planning, putting together a go-kit, and talking with your family about what to expect are important first steps toward personal readiness. Visithttp://ready.gov for more preparedness information.

PMRF is the world's largest instrumented multi-domain range, capable of supporting surface, subsurface, air, and space operations simultaneously. Through dedicated emergency management, interagency drills, and robust mutual aid partnerships, PMRF ensures mission readiness and the safety of its military and civilian workforce, and the broader community.

items.body:
The Air Force has ruled the M18 service pistol is “safe and reliable” after inspecting more than 100,000 of the service’s 9mm pistols, according to a Sept. 2 announcement . Leaders ordered a force-wide inspection after a July 20, 2025, discharge of an M18 killed an on-duty security forces Airman at F.E. Warren Air Force Base, Wyo.

The death of 21-year-old Airman Brayden Lovan was originally believed to be “a result of an accidental discharge ” and fueled safety concerns about the M18—a Sig-Sauer pistol based on its P320 striker-fired weapon. Multiple lawsuits filed against Sig Sauer, mostly by law enforcement officers, have alleged that P320 pistols can discharge unintentionally.

The concerns prompted Air Force Global Strike Command to launch its own investigation and temporarily bar troops from using the M18. The Air Force ordered a service-wide inspection of its “in-use” M18s soon after. Global Strike Command cleared the pistol to return to use in late August 2025 after its own inspections.

More than a year later, the Air Force announced the results of its inspections—though the actual inspection report is dated Jan. 23. As of that date, the service has inspected 113,479 of its 117,864 “in-use” M18s. In total, the service has 125,917 M18s in its inventory—8,053 remain not in use at a depot in Alabama, the report states.

Of the 113,479 M18s inspected, 111,893, or 98.6 percent, were deemed “satisfactory,” the report states. The other 1,586, or 1.4 percent, of the M18s had parts that were “lightly pitted” or required adjustment. Those pistols were categorized as “other than satisfactory,” the report states.

“Some weapons displayed normal wear and tear commensurate with their usage schedule and high rates of manual functioning for skill building during classroom training and daily arming,” the report states. The Air Force “has or will return 1,586 identified during this inspection … with normal wear to ‘serviceable’ condition through standard maintenance procedures.”

The remaining 4,385 “in-use” M18s left to be inspected are “sealed” in extended storage, the report states, adding that commands that own the pistols will be required to complete the inspections.

“Subject matter experts have a high degree of confidence that these final inspections will yield similar findings as the rest of the inventory,” the report states.

Overall, “100 percent of the inspected weapons exhibited no signs of any condition that could have allowed the weapons to experience an ‘uncommanded discharge,’” according to the report.

After an initial investigation into Lovan’s July 20 shooting, criminal investigators learned that Airman 1st Class Marcus White-Allen had concocted a story with two other Airmen to cover up that he fired his M18 pistol into Lovan’s chest.

Laboratory tests have “determined there were no defects in White-Allen’s duty-issued weapon,” according to the Air Force statement. “ Evidence determined White-Allen had his finger on the trigger as he placed the firearm on Lovan’s chest.”

Authorities arrested White-Allen in early August and charged him with involuntary manslaughter, obstruction of justice, and making a false official statement. On Oct. 8, he was found dead in his dormitory, according to the Air Force. Details surrounding White-Allen’s death remain unclear.

Airman 1st Class Sarbjot Badesha and Airmen 1st Class Matthew Rodriguez pleaded guilty to making false statements about the shooting during summary courts martial proceedings on Oct. 30-31, the Air Force said Oct. 31 in a statement. Authorities sentenced Badesha to 30 days in confinement, reduced his rank to E-1 and fined him $1,545. Rodriguez was sentenced to 10 days confinement and 15 days restriction to base. He was also reduced in rank to E-2 and fined $500, according to the statement.

items.body:
JOINT BASE ANDREWS, Md. —Gen. Douglas A. Schiess assumed leadership of the Space Force on Sept. 3, succeeding Gen. B. Chance Saltzman as Chief of Space Operations during a change of responsibility ceremony here.

Schiess is just the third CSO in the Space Force’s history since the service was created in 2019. In his first address to Guardians, he emphasized the important role space has come to play in modern military operations—and the growing threats it attracts from adversaries intent on targeting space assets in orbit and on the ground.

“Every day, our potential adversaries advance their efforts to disrupt, degrade, and destroy our space capabilities, and they try to add to their own capacity to exploit space to their advantage,” Schiess said. “We cannot, we will not let that happen.”

A career space operator, Schiess has performed a number of missions in his career including missile warning, GPS, command and control, and launch. In 2023, he became the first commander of U.S. Space Forces-Space, USSF’s component to the U.S. Space Command combatant command. Most recently, he served as deputy CSO for operations, developing and implementing the policies that guide Space Force operations around the world.

That experience, he said, will inform the way he leads Guardians trained “to operate in the cold, dark vacuum of space” from operations centers on the ground that are also under threat—as evidenced in ongoing operations in the Middle East, where Iran has targeted ground-based space and missile defense infrastructure .

“Our Guardians operate from the ground, some in harm’s way—some in harm’s way today—and they require battlefield skills and the warrior mentality as much as our Soldiers, Sailors, Airmen, Marines, and Coast Guardsmen in our sister services,” he said.

Schiess’ emphasis on the growing threats and the warfighting contributions of Guardians continue themes that his predecessor, Saltzman, repeated often throughout his tenure.

Over the past four years, Saltzman helped grow the Space Force from 8,000 uniformed Guardians to 10,000—and he has positioned the force for even more expansion in the coming years. The service is on a path to double in size to 20,000 Guardians over the next five years, and its $71 billion budget request for fiscal 2027 is more than twice what USSF requested last year, as demand increases for space capabilities.

Speaking during the ceremony, Saltzman said he’s proud of the progress the Space Force has made, evidenced in recent months by its delivery of “critical effects” during multiple operations.

“We delivered critical effects on time and on target under fire, and we sustained that effort,” Saltzman said. “When called to action, the U.S. Space Force was ready, combat capable, and mission effective, and that about says it all.”

Saltzman praised Schiess’ leadership, operational experience, and genuine concern for Guardians, their families, and the joint and allied partners they serve alongside.

“He knows how to build teams, how to drive performance, and how to coax bureaucracies into mission success,” Saltzman said. “He has the expertise to make wise decisions. . . . He cares deeply for the people that do the work.”

In his first message to the force , issued shortly after his swearing in, Schiess harkened back to the Space Force’s early days and looked ahead to the future, calling on Guardians to “capitalize on our foundation and evolve to meet the demands of a new era.”

“As we drive our deliberate growth and execution, we will arm our Guardians to acquire, field, operate, and exploit the full spectrum of capabilities required to secure decisive space superiority,” he said. “Integrating into the Joint Force demands a rapid scaling of both our manpower and space capabilities. We must grow with intention, leveraging our industry partnerships to advance our weapon systems and the way we fight.”

Along with Schiess’ ascension to the service chief job this week, the Department of the Air Force also welcomed its assistant secretary for space acquisition and integration, Erich Hernandez-Baquero, who was sworn in at the Pentagon on Aug. 31 . Hernandez-Baquero, who will oversee a growing space acquisition portfolio, fills a position that has been vacant since January 2025, though several officials have served in an acting capacity.

items.body:
The U.S. Army awarded a $464.8 million production contract to AeroVironment, Inc., this week for the Enduring-High Energy Laser program (E-HEL), marking the first production contract for a directed energy system in the U.S. military’s history, the company stated in a release Wednesday.

Rather than deploying missiles to shoot down unmanned aircraft, the E-HEL fires a laser beam at its targets and can reload its magazine through the system’s power supply, according to the Army.

“This first-of-its-kind directed energy program will enable our formations to defeat unmanned systems and dominate from the outset,” Vice Chief of Staff of the Army General Christopher LaNeve said in an Army statement. “Pairing human ingenuity with advanced technology is what ensures our Army will continue to outpace America’s adversaries.”

Under the Other Transaction Agreement, AV will deliver dozens of 30 kW LOCUST laser weapons capable of taking down smaller drones that fit within what the Defense Department characterizes as groups one through three . Those include miniature UAVs comparable to the Air Force’s Wasp III to the Army’s RQ-7B Shadow in the larger class.

The E-HEL production announcement also notches a much-needed win for the service’s laser program, following soldiers’ disappointing feedback on the Army’s Directed Energy Maneuver Short-Range Air Defense (DE M-SHORAD) performance in the Middle East.

While those prototypes were tailored for the Stryker combat vehicle, AV’s LOCUST X3 laser weapon is platform-agnostic and can fit on the Army’s Joint Light Tactical Vehicle (JLTV).

The E-HEL program builds on the success of the Army Multi-Purpose High Energy Laser (AMP-HEL) prototypes currently in use by U.S. soldiers.

The contract follows LOCUST’s successful testing at White Sands Missile Range , led by Joint Interagency Task Force 401 (JIATF-401) and PAE Fires, which demonstrated safe, effective counter-drone operations in U.S. airspace and directly enabled a DOW–FAA safety agreement validating the system for domestic use.

items.author: Chris Gordon

items.body:
Air Force B-52 Stratofortress bombers landed at a northern Australian air base this week, a major display of the U.S. military’s ability to project force in the Pacific.

Multiple B-52s landed at Royal Australian Air Force Base Tindal in the country’s Northern Territory on Sept. 1, according to official Air Force imagery released Sept. 3.

The joint military-civilian airfield near the town of Katherine, which the Pentagon plans to use as a launching pad for operations in the Pacific, has undergone a $1.1 billion upgrade in recent years.

That work enables it to support the deployment of a half-dozen B-52s, giving the U.S. more locations to stage bombers in the region amid China’s growing military might.

The base also houses Australian F-35A Lightning stealth fighter jets and MQ-4C Triton remotely piloted surveillance aircraft.

Australia is south of the U.S. territory of Guam, where Andersen Air Force Base serves as America’s current bomber hub in the Western Pacific. RAAF Base Tindal would give the U.S. Air Force more basing options for long-range missions in the region.

“Operating from RAAF Base Tindal marks our ability to project, sustain, and regenerate decisive airpower across an expanding extended network,” states one photo caption released by Pacific Air Forces. The deployment from the base “deepens our partnership and interoperability” and “highlights our shared commitment to regional stability, ensuring our forces remain agile and responsive in support of a Free and Open Indo-Pacific,” PACAF added in other captions.

Air Force Global Strike Command and the Eighth Air Force, which oversees the nation’s bomber force, declined to comment, citing operational security, and referred questions to Pacific Air Forces on Sept. 2 when asked about the deployment. PACAF did not immediately respond to a request for comment. It is unclear how long the bombers will be deployed to the region and how many aircraft are operating from Australia. The bombers hail from the 2nd Bomb Wing at Barksdale Air Force Base, La.

Multiple wargames on potential conflicts with China have highlighted the strategic and operational value of Australia’s airbases and naval facilities, said retired Col. Mark Gunzinger, a former B-52 pilot and deputy assistant secretary of defense for forces transformation and resources.

“That has been a constant in our wargames: using Australia’s multiple airfields—and not just in northern Australia but in the south too—to generate long-range bomber strikes and tanker sorties to support bomber and fighter operations,” said Gunzinger, the Director of Future Concepts and Capability Assessments at AFA’s Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies.

“China has a limited number of very long-range ballistic missiles that can reach U.S. air forces stationed at Diego Garcia, in Australia, and other air bases that are not located along the First Island Chain.” Bombers’ longer ranges would allow them to be stationed at airfields even further from China if necessary, Gunzinger added.

Washington and Canberra are increasingly aligned under the AUKUS security pact, which also includes the United Kingdom. The agreement will give U.S. nuclear-powered subs to Australia and allow the U.S. to stage subs out of Australia starting next year. Conceived under the Biden administration, AUKUS has also been embraced by the second Trump administration.

Australian Deputy Prime Minister and Defense Minister Richard Marles met with Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth at the Pentagon on Sept. 2 to commemorate the 75th anniversary of the ANZUS Treaty, a mutual defense pact, during which the two defense chiefs “discussed how both nations will continue to advance the alliance and strengthen deterrence in the Pacific.”

“The Secretary noted the alignment between U.S. and Australian National Defense Strategies and also acknowledged that Canberra recognizes the gravity of maintaining a favorable balance of power in the region to ensure that both countries remain safe and prosperous,” the Pentagon said in a readout provided from the meeting. “Both leaders agreed to accelerate force posture initiatives at Australian bases, bolster cooperation in combined logistics, and build greater interoperability through joint exercises.”

The U.S. has operated fighters and bombers from other Royal Australian Air Force Bases, such as RAAF Base Amberley , and the two countries conduct the biennial Talisman Saber, one of the largest and most complex military training exercises held. By 2030, the U.S. Navy expects some 2,300 Americans to be based in Western Australia.

“What we’re seeing is a real increase in U.S. posture in Australia,” said Zack Cooper, a senior fellow and expert on U.S. strategy in Asia at the American Enterprise Institute. “Sometimes it can take a really long time to build out the infrastructure, but in this case, I think we’re seeing the U.S. and Australia move pretty quickly on both the air and the naval side. I think it’s emblematic of the step-up in effort we’re seeing from both Canberra and Washington.”

“The U.S. needs to diversify the locations from which it can operate air and naval assets. Australia’s northern bases do that on the air side and the naval facilities in Perth are critical on the nuclear submarine side,” he added.

Equipping a base to handle large bombers with heavy payloads is no small task: runways must be long, sturdy, and adequate, with ramp space, fuel infrastructure, and safe weapons storage facilities.

“That can all drive some considerable investment in airfields, which Australia has made and continues to invest in to bolster regional deterrence,” Gunzinger said.

items.body:
A bipartisan group of lawmakers is pushing the Army to explain why it is shuttering a specialized drone battalion less than a year after establishing it, a move that comes as conflicts across the world have become increasingly defined by unmanned aerial systems and electronic warfare.

The 600-member “Unmanned Assault Battalion,” created as part of the 173rd Airborne Brigade , was charged with learning tactics and skills from Ukraine’s more-than four-year fight against Russia and applying them to the U.S. military. In a letter , legislators expressed concern that eliminating the battalion was another sign of the Defense Department’s “uneven and inconsistent” support to Europe and Ukraine, and they questioned how the U.S. would continue to learn drone warfare from the Ukraine theater.

“We have deep concerns that eliminating this specialized drone unit will limit our ability to learn from allies, particularly the Ukrainian Armed Forces, and hinder our efforts to modernize drone warfare at the speed necessary to compete on the modern battlefield,” Sens. Jeanne, Shahee, Thom Tillis, Angus King and Rep. Michael Turner, said in the Sept. 1 letter, provided by Sen. Shaheen’s office.

“This specialized unit was a prudent response in a moment when the character of warfare is changing faster than a conventional formation’s ability to adapt,” the lawmakers said after asking if the decision to close the unit was made by the Army or based on guidance from Defense Department leadership. They asked for an explanation by Sept. 21.

The unit is expected to return to its airborne infantry mission after participating in the multinational Exercise Saber Junction this month.

In the letter, addressed to Acting Army Chief of Staff. Gen. Christopher LaNeve and outgoing Army Secretary Dan Driscoll, legislators said they understood the move to be a result of Gen. LaNeve’s “back to basics” message , where he ordered the force to focus on its primary combat mission.

The Army has seen a massive leadership shakeup as Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has fired over a dozen top leaders. Former Army Chief of Staff, Gen. Randy George, who championed drone innovation through his Transformation in Contact initiative, was ousted at Hegseth’s behest. He has not yet nominated a successor.

Driscoll, who supported modernization measures and acquisition reform, resigned on short notice this week amid friction with Hegseth. His resignation further thins the Army’s top ranks as the country remains locked into a war with Iran that has now stretched over six months amid missile stockpile shortages and extended deployments.

items.body:
The base cost of an F-35A, the Air Force variant of the Joint Strike Fighter , is going up 11.5 percent from $82.5 million to $92 million for the latest lots of the fifth-generation aircraft, Air & Space Forces Magazine has confirmed.

A spokesperson for the F-35 Joint Program Office gave cost estimates for each F-35 variant, averaged across Lots 18 and 19, in current-year dollars. A recent Pentagon acquisition report gave the estimates in 2012 dollars, when the program was rebaselined. The new figures give insight how inflation is affecting the program.

Manufacturer Lockheed Martin lists the price of F-35 variants for Lots 15 through 17 on its website.

The totals are average flyaway costs, which refer to all the basic costs it takes to produce one aircraft. The JPO confirmed those price tags include the cost of the jets’ engines and radars, which are provided to manufacturer Lockheed Martin as government-furnished equipment.

The cost of the F-35A went up the most in recent lots, at 11.5 percent, with the F-35B almost identical in terms of percentage growth. The F-35C went up the least, at just 8.5 percent.

But the F-35A remains the cheapest and least complex variant of the three. The F-35B—the short takeoff and vertical landing variant flown by the Marine Corps—is the most expensive and complicated, given its unique swiveling engine nozzle and hovering capabilities. And the F-35C, flown by both the Marine Corps and the Navy, is closer in price to the F-35B and has bigger wings than the F-35A to help with carrier landings, as well as folding wingtips to help with storage in close quarters.

The revelation of the price tags for the F-35s’ upcoming lots—the highest in the nearly $2 trillion program’s history—follows the Pentagon’s release of a modernized selected acquisition report which said the total estimated acquisition cost for the F-35, including both airframes and engines, had grown more than 10 percent to $536.2 billion.

The selected acquisition report, which was released in August, pointed to inflation and critical upgrades as causes of the F-35’s cost growth. But the report only included flyways costs for the three variants in 2012 dollars, leaving the full effects of inflation unclear. Those costs were:

$78 million for the F-35A, up 7.3 percent from the previous report in 2023.

$110.3 million for the F-35B, up 10.5 percent from the previous report.

$93.4 million for the F-35C, up 6.6 percent from the previous report.

The fact that the actual costs are seeing greater percentage increases could suggest inflation is having a significant effect on the jet’s price tag.

Lockheed officials have been sounding warnings about the growing effects of inflation on the F-35 for some time now.

Greg Ulmer, then-president of Lockheed Martin Aeronautics, told Defense One in July 2024 that keeping the F-35’s price under the rate of inflation would be challenging for Lots 18 and 19.

“Inflation is real,” Ulmer said at the Farnborough Air Show in England. “The cost of raw materials has gone up. The cost of everything has gone up, so there is just inflation pressure in the system.”

The JPO, Lockheed, and other F-35 contractors have also been working on adding more capabilities to the jet, including additional computing and processing power under the Technology Refresh 3 program and additional weapons, sensor, and sensor fusion capabilities as part of the Block 4 effort.

The JPO pointed to information in the selected acquisition report when asked for comment on the Lots 18 and 19 cost growth. Lockheed Martin said in a response to a query that the recent acquisition report shows the program is moving into full-rate production, resuming high-volume development deliveries, and growing globally.

“It also shows that the hard work has shifted from proving the basic aircraft to executing major modernization, improving fleet readiness, and controlling long-term sustainment and integration costs,” a Lockheed spokesperson said.

The JPO had previously declined to release the cost for each variant in current-year dollars and said those numbers were considered controlled unclassified information. The office eventually released the figures after further queries from Air & Space Forces Magazine.

The JPO and Lockheed Martin in September 2025 struck a final “definitized” deal for Lots 18 and 19, which would buy 296 fighters for nearly $24.3 billion . That deal was for just the airframe and did not include engine costs, meaning the average cost of just the airframe across all variants will be $82.4 million.

The post What Each F-35 Variant Really Costs Right Now appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .

items.title: Defense firms soar on ample military spending, testing manufacturing schemes
items.author: Defense News staff
items.summary: The year 2025 was another record setter for global defense companies, so much so that production bottlenecks in Western nations — not the usual industry lamentations about lacking government spending — began creeping up as the key problem many NATO countries are facing today. items.body:
The year 2025 was another record setter for global defense companies, so much so that production bottlenecks in Western nations — not the usual industry lamentations about lacking government spending — began creeping up as the key problem many NATO countries are facing today.

Companies in the United States and Europe rode a wave of significant defense-spending increases on both sides of the Atlantic. In Europe, individual national budget increases, as well as the European Union’s increasing involvement in brokering and financing joint procurement, continued to increase the revenue of defense industry players large and small.

In the United States, the 2025 Reconciliation Act is set to pump most of the legislation’s total $156 billion into acquisition — on top of the regular defense budget of roughly $900 billion for that year.

“Now, it’ll take years for that enacted money to actually flow to the companies and to their financial statements,” said Mark Cancian, a senior adviser in the defense analysis program at the Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies. “But it will be a big boost for many companies.”

Click here to view the 2025 Defense News Top 100

In Europe, the trajectory is perhaps more immediate, as governments spooked by Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 began dialing up their military expenditures drastically years ago.

Besides absorbing the overall plus-up in the amount of money available, companies on the continent have rewired their business strategies to align with a preference for European-made equipment by many European governments, though the massive influx of cash on all sides obfuscates whether European companies have meaningfully cut into the bottom lines of U.S. defense giants.

More money on both sides of the pond

The latest Defense News Top 100 ranking of global defense companies bears out the overall upward trend, with companies posting higher annual defense revenues, a combined $700 billion compared with $629 billion in the prior year, a 11.3% increase.

The first four spots of our latest ranking continue to be in the hands of U.S. firms, with Lockheed Martin in the top spot with $72.1 billion in annual defense revenue, followed by RTX ($46 billion), General Dynamics ($39.4 billion) and Northrop Grumman ($37 billion), in that order.

Britain-based BAE Systems, which has a sizable U.S. operation, is the first non-American company in the lineup, creeping up one spot into number five over last year’s ranking, with $36 billion in revenue reported.

Boeing’s defense segment similarly climbed one position, into slot number six with $35.7 billion in revenue, as did L3Harris ($17.4 billion), which now places eighth.

In between sits a Chinese entrant, Aviation Industry Corporation of China, at $32.3 billion.

Click here to view the 2025 Defense News Top 100

On the heels of that company begins a lineup of firms from all over the world, with European outfits continuing to inch upwards — the big players Leonardo, Airbus and Thales placing 9, 10 and 12, respectively.

Perhaps no company represents the European defense uptick as much as Germany’s Rheinmetall, which reported $11.2 billion in 2025 annual revenue, up from $8.3 billion in the previous year. The company now sits at number 15 on the list, up from 18 in the prior year.

The firm has, over the years, branched out its operations into virtually all domains of war — land, air, naval, space, cyber and unmanned — from Europe to Australia, and has embraced the formerly low-brow segment of explosives and ammunition.

That category, which includes artillery shells, missiles and air-defense interceptors, has seen unprecedented demand in all NATO countries, based on the experiences since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Air defense competitions on the rise

The air defense category is also where the biggest shortfalls lie. Companies have expanded their supply chain setups in recent years to build artillery shells, urgently needed in Ukraine to shoot over immediate front lines’ robot-dominated no-go zones for infantry.

But what’s still lacking are sufficient interceptor missiles and drones to defend against Russian missiles fired at Ukrainian cities.

With the Patriot air defense complex — radars, launchers and interceptors — in the hands of U.S. firms, European and Ukrainian officials have begun thinking through alternatives to the scarce equipment.

Offerers include the Israeli companies involved in that country’s anti-missile architecture, with Elbit ranking 21 on the list, Israeli Aerospace Industries at 27 and Rafael at 30, as well as pan-European firm MBDA at 26 and Germany’s Diehl at 58, up from 82 last year.

Companies with a naval shipbuilding portfolio, such as General Dynamics, Huntington Ingalls (ranking 13, at $12.3 billion annual revenue, up from 16) and South Korea’s Hanwha (rank 16, at $10.4 billion, up from 22), have been lifted by a favorable tide of capital-intensive naval modernization projects worldwide.

In the U.S., defense officials and lawmakers have envisioned a new armada of warships and icebreakers, dedicating a whopping $29 billion for shipbuilding in the 2025 Reconciliation Act alone.

“The Biden administration, and now the Trump administration, have just been pouring money into shipbuilding — way beyond what the industry can absorb,” said Cancian. “And then they’re talking about building another shipyard to produce all these ships that have now been funded,” he added, leaving shipbuilders with order books filled into the 2030s or beyond.

Defense spending as an ‘engine’?

Production bottlenecks for defense components, combined with economic woes in civilian industry sectors, have led to some new creative arrangements.

In Europe, some automotive companies and rail car makers have turned their factory floors into production sites for drones and counter-drone equipment.

The rush to re-arm, based on the worry that Russia might try a Ukraine-style attack elsewhere, has prompted political leaders in Europe to tout what they consider secondary economic effects of the defense bonanza.

Defense officials in the U.K. published figures in August, for example, that said the 2024-25 period saw British weapons and ammunition manufacturing jobs rise by 51%, “part of a wider 26,000 increase” in defense-supported roles nationwide.

Click here to view the 2025 Defense News Top 100

“The increase underlines defense as an engine for growth and the move towards a resilient industrial base, proving that investment in the U.K.’s security is investment in the U.K.’s prosperity,” reads an Aug. 20 statement by the Ministry of Defence.

Some Turkish companies, meanwhile, representing a country with a government mandate for making defense equipment at home rather than importing it, made the latest Top 100 list again, improving positions in some cases. Aselsan jumped from spot 43 to 40 on roughly $4.5 billion in reported annual revenue, and Roketsan gained seven ranks, on $2.4 billion, landing at spot 64.

Similarly, Polish state-owned armaments group PGZ jumped from rank 54 in 2024 figures to number 41 in the latest accounting, based on $4.4 billion in revenue last year.

The Polish government has set out plans to create one of NATO’s most powerful armies in Europe, and local weapons programs are typically designed to include Warsaw’s go-to producer as a key partner.

Meanwhile, the collection of Ukrainian defense companies under the umbrella of Ukroboronprom improved their ranking to spot number 36, up from 49 last year, with a reported revenue of $4.6 billion in 2025.

The country’s defense industry over the past years has put the Kyiv government in a position to provide armaments to its forces that the country previously had to import, often with operational limitations attached.

So much has the Ukrainian defense industry gained in expertise that allied militaries are itching to incorporate its know-how into their own supply chains.

Looking ahead, there is more spending expected, and more business for relevant defense companies, in the field of air and missile defense, said Cancian. Much of that will be connected to whatever the Trump administration’s Golden Dome program will entail, he noted.

Golden Dome wildcard

The controversial Golden Dome effort will consist of a sweeping suite of sensors and interceptors — stationed on Earth, in space and everywhere in between — that would make the United States almost impervious to aerial attacks of any kind, the theory goes.

Details have been scant on its exact architecture, and companies are searching for avenues into what they suspect will be a generational chunk of government spending in the hundreds of billions of dollars.

“We still don’t really know what it is,” Cancian said, adding the lack of clarity could make the whole project an increasingly hard sell as time goes by.

On the whole, the analyst said, there is so much defense spending on the books that the U.S. government, for its part, isn’t forced to choose between buying legacy weaponry and new technology.

“The thing that struck me most — I come out at this from a program budget perspective — is that there was enough money to do both,” he said.

Turning the influx of defense money into meaningfully improved defenses will be a top oversight job for politicians. And industry will have to be disciplined to get its ducks in a row to contend with order backlogs and production bottlenecks.

As PricewaterhouseCoopers analyst Scott Thompson noted in a recent performance analysis of the aerospace and defense sectors, “In a market where demand is not the constraint, execution is the differentiator.”

items.title: Key milestone reached for future Navy support ship as names of sister ships announced
items.summary: RFA Resurgent's keel laying ceremony took place at Navantia UK's Appledore shipyard today, as her sister ships' names, RFA Reliant and RFA Resourceful, were revealed during the ceremony.
items.body:
RFA Resurgent, the first of three new Fleet Solid Support ships, begins to take shape with keel laying as names for sister ships, RFA Reliant and RFA Resourceful, are announced.

The Fleet Solid Support programme is expected to create around 1,200 UK shipyard jobs and hundreds of apprenticeships, boosting sovereign shipbuilding in Navantia UK’s Appledore and Belfast shipyards.

RFA Resurgent is due to enter service in the early 2030s, supporting Royal Navy vessels at sea including carrier strike group operations.

The Royal Navy’s ability to operate further and for longer at sea took a step forward today, as a key milestone was reached in the build of the first of its future solid support ship fleet.

RFA Resurgent, the first-in-class of three new Fleet Solid Support (FSS) ships being delivered to the Royal Fleet Auxiliary (RFA), had her keel laid today. Held at Navantia UK’s Appledore shipyard, the keel laying ceremony marked the point at which RFA Resurgent’s structure formally begins to take shape. The names of her sister ships, RFA Reliant and RFA Resourceful, were also announced during the ceremony by the Head of the RFA, Commodore Sam Shattock.

The FSS programme will see around £100M invested into Navantia UK’s shipyards in Belfast and Appledore, Devon - creating 1,200 jobs and hundreds of apprenticeships and supporting reindustrialisation.

Once in service, RFA Resurgent and her two sister ships will deliver munitions, spares, food and other essential supplies to Royal Navy vessels at sea, allowing the fleet to remain deployed for longer, including in support of carrier strike group operations.

Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, Luke Pollard MP said:

The Royal Fleet Auxiliary are the backbone of our Royal Navy and these new ships will keep our navy ready to operate at range for longer.

Seeing the steel cut for RFA Resurgent last year was a proud moment, and today’s keel laying shows real momentum behind this vital programme.

This investment is helping bolster UK shipbuilding, backing thousands of skilled jobs and apprenticeships in Appledore, Belfast and beyond.

A specially commissioned coin was placed within the ship’s structure and will be presented to the Captain and crew when the ship is ready to sail - in keeping with tradition.

Keith Bethell, Director Maritime Environment at the NAD Group, said:

Today’s keel lay is a significant stride forward in delivering the support our Royal Navy needs to operate at pace and at range, wherever it is needed.

Through the NAD Group’s work procuring this capability alongside Navantia UK and the wider supply chain, we are proud to be supporting our armed forces and backing British shipbuilding and skilled jobs.

Each ship will have a core RFA crew of 101, with accommodation provided for an additional 80 personnel operating helicopters, boats, or performing other roles when required. Delivery of the first Fleet Solid Support ship is on track, with RFA Resurgent expected to enter service with the RFA in the early 2030s.

Commodore Sam Shattock, Head of the RFA, said:

Today’s keel laying marks another important step in the delivery of RFA Resurgent and the wider Fleet Solid Support programme. Seeing construction progress here in Appledore demonstrates the momentum behind a project that will provide the Royal Fleet Auxiliary with world-class capabilities to sustain Royal Navy operations across the globe.

The commemorative coin placed beneath the keel continues a proud maritime tradition, linking this modern programme with generations of shipbuilders and seafarers who have gone before us. I am delighted that apprentices from both Navantia UK and the Royal Fleet Auxiliary have been part of this occasion, representing the future of UK shipbuilding and the future of the RFA.

Construction of ship modules is now taking place at Navantia UK’s Appledore yard, along with its Harland & Wolff shipyard in Belfast and Navantia’s yards in Spain. Final assembly, integration and trials of the ships will take place at their Harland & Wolff shipyard in Belfast.

Donato Martínez, CEO of Navantia UK, said:

Today’s keel laying marks the formal start of assembly of the first Fleet Solid Support ship and an important moment for Appledore, where shipbuilding has returned to a yard with more than 170 years of history.

FSS is rebuilding sovereign industrial capability in the UK, creating skilled jobs, developing apprentices and strengthening the supply chain for future naval programmes, including the autonomous and uncrewed platforms of the future Hybrid Navy.

This milestone shows what sustained investment and close partnership between government and industry can deliver, and we are focused on maintaining that momentum as the first ship takes shape.

This programme forms part of the Government’s Defence Investment Plan and its wider £298 billion investment in Defence.

items.body:
The U.S. Navy has experienced some considerable setbacks in recent months, from a power failure on a destroyer in the South China Sea to morale issues aboard the aircraft carrier USS Lincoln. Still, the service has been buoyed by a nationwide recognition that shipbuilding has too long been neglected and the current administration seems to have a variety of innovative maritime strategy concepts, encompassing a new vision for the fleet.

Among these ideas, none have been more controversial than the proposed Trump-class battleship .

Proponents argue that this new capital ship would bring concentrated fighting power with new high-tech weapons and large magazines that could fight independently and also withstand substantial punishment in battle. With its currently planned nuclear propulsion, moreover these behemoths could patrol for extended periods without the need to refuel.

Critics have taken aim at the project’s enormous expense, as well as the feasibility of the proposed design that is characterized as over-ambitious.

Into this roiling debate, it is instructive to survey a rather different perspective: What do the Chinese make of this project? An Aug. 21 article in China National Defense News [中国国防报] provides some initial insights into how America’s chief global rival is assessing this potentially major change in direction for the U.S. Navy surface fleet.

This article, published in an official paper of the Peoples Liberation Army (PLA) does note that the ship could have the advantages that “large vessels can continue to execute certain combat missions even when communications are jammed, and their hulls offer superior damage resistance compared to small or medium-sized ships.” It notes that smaller, distributed platforms could overly “rely on stable data links.” In addition, it’s worth observing that this rendering does note that the planned U.S. battleship would have nuclear propulsion, and would possibly also carry nuclear-armed missiles.

Nevertheless, the Chinese analysis, mirroring many Western evaluations, is suffused with ample skepticism.

For 15 Trump-class battleships built between 2028 and 2056, the costs would amount to $275 billion, with the lead class carrying the price tag of $23.4 billion. The report says that cost is 55% higher due to the change from conventional to nuclear propulsion and terms this price as “exorbitant.” Illustrating some familiarity with nuclear power issues, the analysis adds that “nuclear waste disposal and vessel dismantling following retirement are not included” in the $275 billion estimate.

“Unfinalized designs and insufficient technological maturity” are also flagged as potential major problem that may cause delays and cost overruns. Potentially carrying rail guns, hypersonic weapons, as well as lasers, this critique seems quite valid. As the PLA assessment states: “This ‘build the platform first, install equipment later’ approach could increase the risks.” The piece cites the examples of the both the Zumwalt-class destroyer and the Littoral Combat Ship (LCS) as relevant examples of recent problematic programs.

Notably, the Chinese article is also particularly attuned to potential shifts in the basic U.S. Navy warfighting doctrinal paradigm.

The article observes: “This design differs from the Distributed Maritime Operations concept that the U.S. Navy has been advancing in recent years. The theory of distributed maritime operations emphasizes the dispersal of detection, command, and strike capabilities across multiple nodes … to mitigate the impact that damage to a few large vessels would have on the entire formation.”

In a closely related point, the PLA article also broaches the question of whether large surface combatants are simply too vulnerable to quiet submarines, hypersonic missiles, and “drone swarms.”

Apparently quite aware of major difficulties in U.S. shipbuilding, the Chinese military assessment adds that leading American shipyards “are currently facing average delays of five years, with the delivery cycle for a single ship extending from approximately five years in the early 2000’s to about eleven years today.”

Noting that the new battleship program could have cascading results for other high priority U.S. Navy programs, the article concludes: “Assembly of nuclear-powered battleships … could further slow the construction of aircraft carriers and submarines.” These Chinese strategists are no doubt aware such a delay would further impact the Asia-Pacific naval balance.

China itself has indicated interest in nuclear-powered surface vessels. Thus, they have thoroughly investigated the newly renovated Russian battle cruiser Admiral Nakihimov.

Yet it is would be foolhardy to invest in such ambitious platforms for the U.S. Navy at a time when the service confronts so many shipbuilding challenges and when the nation also faces an inevitable process of belt-tightening. Perhaps some of America’s allies can experiment with the new battleship concept. But the U.S. Navy will be well advised to go toward its time-tested strengths, especially in undersea warfare, but also in the emergent domain of drones.

Overall, America’s sea service must bring its force structure into alignment with a new strategy appropriate to the multipolar world that involves reducing expensive “presence” missions and embracing more cost-effective hedging.

That will most likely mean a less high-profile role for surface combatants and thus recognizing the reality that the Trump-class battleship will most likely never get built.

Certainly, this Chinese military article implies that at least some Chinese strategists are eager for the U.S. to pursue that extravagant project, knowing that it is folly and would thus weaken Beijing’s chief rival.

Lyle Goldstein is director of the China Initiative at Brown University’s Watson School and concurrently serves as director of the Asia Program at the think-tank Defense Priorities.

items.title: Guidance: Defence Employer Recognition Scheme
items.summary: The Employer Recognition Scheme (ERS) encourages employers to support defence and inspire other organisations to do the same.
items.body:
About the scheme

The Defence Employer Recognition Scheme ( ERS ) encourages employers to support defence and inspire others to do the same. The scheme encompasses Bronze, Silver and Gold awards for employer organisations that pledge, demonstrate or advocate support to defence and the armed forces community, and align their values with the Armed Forces Covenant .

The ERS is designed primarily to recognise private sector support although public sector organisations such as the emergency services, local authorities, NHS trusts and executive agencies are also eligible to be recognised.

Pledge your organisation’s support via the Bronze award or express your interest in a Silver or Gold award via the links below.

Privacy policy

You can read our Privacy policy to find out more about how we process data.

Bronze award

Bronze award holders must have:

Signed the AFC and registered their interest for a Bronze award (via the ERS website).

Confirmed their understanding of the AFC and ERS and what it means to be a supporter of the Armed Forces community with the appointed DRM.

Informed their workforce of their positive support for the Armed Forces community.

Desirable Criteria. Factors which add value to an application. Note that the description of these allows for an assessment of evidence in the context of the scale, business model and market sector of the employer. The employer is willing to consider:

How to develop a suitable HR framework to enable Reserve mobilisation for members of their work force.

Provide additional leave for Reservists (i.e. Part Time Volunteer Reserves) to conduct training.

How they would promote volunteering and support to the Cadet movement through official Cadet Force channels.

How they ensure that Service personnel/Armed Forces community are not unfairly disadvantaged as part of their recruiting and selection processes.

Nominate your organisation for a Bronze award

View the ERS Bronze award holders

Silver award

Silver award holders in addition to Bronze Criteria must have:

ERS Bronze Award status and have held it with sufficient time to have put in place the necessary essential policies and evidence to support their application. It would be unusual for an organisation to achieve Silver status within 12 months of gaining Bronze.

Proactively demonstrate that Service personnel and Armed Forces community are not unfairly disadvantaged as part of their recruiting and selection processes.

Actively ensure that their workforce is aware of their positive policies towards the Armed Forces community. E.g. Internally publicised positive HR policy on Reserves in their workforce. In the case where no HR policy exists this should be demonstrated by specific references in job descriptions/organisation’s website.

Support Active Reservists (PTVRs) by:

Having Policy in place to support mobilisations or have made a commitment evidenced by their DRM that they understand the mobilisation process and would support a mobilisation if practicable. E.g. Employers of reservists must be aware of the role of Unit Employment Support Officers (UESO) and how they support the Reservists in their work forces.

Demonstrated support to their training by providing at least 5 days additional annual leave (ideally paid).

A proactive relationship with their DRM, which can be demonstrated through various interactions, including but not limited to personal contact, automated communications, and engagement with supporting products or resources.

The employer must allow flexibility for employees who are Cadet Force Adult Volunteers to fit their working hours in with their volunteering.

Desirable Criteria. Factors which add value to an application. Note that the description of these allows for an assessment of evidence in the context of the scale, business model and market sector of the employer. The employer is willing to consider:

Scoping opportunities to support the Cadet movement (via official Cadet Force channels) through the following example activities: sponsorship, supporting the development of cadets’ wider skills to enhance their future opportunities; or providing employment advice and guidance.

Employ at least one individual from the Armed Forces community .

Hosting a Reserve recruiting event on their premises in partnership with a local Reserve Unit or Military Command recruiting teams.

Have inclusive policy in place to support Strategic Reserves (those with an Ex-Regular and Callout liability).

View the 2026 ERS Silver Award Holders

Gold award

Gold award holders in addition to Silver Criteria must have:Hold ERS Silver Award and have held it with sufficient time to have put in place the necessary essential policies and evidence to support their application. It would be very unusual for an organisation to achieve Gold status within 12 months of gaining Silver.

Be an exemplar within their sector, advocating for the AFC and or ERS to partner organisations, suppliers and customers with tangible positive results. E.g. demonstrate proactive steps/activity and clear success in encouraging partner organisations and their supply chain to engage with and sign the AFC, and or mentor others in progressing through the ERS .

Actively encourage a positive workplace environment for Active Reservists (Part Time Volunteer Reserves) by ensuring that positive policies in support of Reservists within the workforce are communicated to line managers and support their training by providing at least 10 days additional paid leave annually.

Demonstrate support to the Cadet movement by committing resources to improving the outcomes for cadets. This is to be achieved by verifying they deliver one or a combination of the following through official Cadet Force channels:

1) Sponsorship (e.g. for additional resources, competitions, events and specific activities such as overseas expeditions);

2) Supporting the development of cadets’ wider skills to enhance their future opportunities;

3) Providing employment advice and guidance.

Promote volunteering with the Cadet Forces by having policies in place that cater to offer additional paid or unpaid leave to employees who are Cadet Force Adult Volunteers.

Engaged with CTP to support recruitment of Service leavers and have registered with the Forces Families Jobs website.

Desirable Criteria. Factors which add value to an application. Note that the description of these allows for an assessment of evidence in the context of the scale, business model and market sector of the employer. The employer is willing to consider:

Support to Reserve Service and the wider Armed Forces community through internal and external communications, amplifying DRM social media messaging around Armed Forces Week, Reserves Day, ERS Gold /Silver announcements etc.

Actively finding out the numbers of Reservists employed and have a declared target for the number of Reservists within their workforce. Ideally, they will have relationships with the relevant Unit Employment Support Officers (UESO) for reserve units in their local area.

If there are Reservists within the workforce, the employer has positively engaged with them on how the company would support their mobilisation.

Host a Reserve recruiting event on their premises in partnership with a Reserve Unit or Military Command Recruiting Teams.

Where scale and business models permit, the employer should actively encourage and support an internal Armed Forces community network within their organisation.

View the 2026 ERS Gold award holders

Nomination and award process

Employers can sign up themselves for each award.

Nominations will be validated to determine the level of defence personnel employment within the nominated organisation and to check that the organisation has signed the Armed Forces Covenant .

Once the nomination has been validated it will be considered by a selection board at national level for gold awards and regional level for silver awards. The selection boards will be a panel chaired by a senior military officer and they will consider each nomination against the award criteria. Organisations selected for gold and silver awards will be formally notified in writing and invited to the relevant award event.
